{{Short description|Flemish Christian missionary to China (1651–1729)}}
{{lead too short|date=January 2018}}
'''François Noël''', [[Society of Jesus|SJ]] (18 August 1651 – 17 September 1729) was a [[Flemish people|Flemish]] [[Jesuits|Jesuit]], [[poet]], [[dramatist]], and [[Jesuit China missions|missionary]] to the [[Qing Empire]]. Nöel unsuccessfully testified in support of Chinese converts to [[Catholic Church|Catholicism]] retaining [[ancestral veneration]] during the [[Chinese Rites controversy]] but also opposed incorporating other elements of [[Confucianism]] into Catholic practice. He also achieved notability for translating several Chinese texts for European audiences.

{{anchor|Names}}

==Name==
{{chinese
|altname=Wei Fangji |t2={{linktext|衛|方|濟}} |s2={{linktext|卫|方|济}} |p2=Wèi Fāngjì |w2=Wei Fang-chi
}}
Noël wrote his translations in [[Latin]], in which his name [[Latinization of names|appears as]] '''Franciscus Noel'''. He is also known by its [[anglicization]] as '''Francis Noel'''. He was known to the Chinese as '''Wei Fangji'''.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}}

==Life==
===Early life===
François Noël was a [[Flemish people|Fleming]]<ref name=ruleno1/> born on 18 August 1651 in [[Hestrud]], [[French Hainault|Hainault]], [[Kingdom of France|France]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} He joined the [[Jesuits]] at the age of nineteen on 30 September 1670 in [[Tournai]],{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} which had just been returned to France from the [[Spanish Netherlands]] two years before under the terms of the [[War of Devolution]]'s [[Treaty of Aachen (1668)|Treaty of Aachen]]. He was a teacher of [[Latin grammar|grammar]] and [[rhetoric]] for several years.<ref name=ruleno2>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA138 138]}}.</ref> He studied [[Christian theology|theology]], [[History of mathematics#Mathematics during the Scientific Revolution|mathematics]], and [[History of astronomy#Renaissance Period|astronomy]] at the [[University of Douai]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}}

{{anchor|China mission|Jesuit China mission}}

===In China===
[[File:The tomb of Xuguangqi.jpg|thumb|left|200px|The [[Chinese tomb|tomb]] of [[Xu Guangqi]] (d. 1633) in [[Shanghai]]'s [[Xujiahui]] neighborhood]]
[[File:Paradigma XV Provinciarum &c.png|thumb|right|200px|China as known to the Jesuits {{c.|1687}}.]]
[[File:Carte la plus generale et qui comprend la Chine, la Tartarie Chinoise, et le Thibet (1734).jpg|thumb|right|200px|China as known to the Jesuits {{c.|1735}}.]]
{{further|Jesuit China missions}}
He wanted to join the [[Jesuit Japan mission|Japan mission]] but by this point [[Christianity in Japan|Christianity]] (and European visitors generally) had been banned within the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] for many years.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} He nonetheless traveled to [[Lisbon]], [[Kingdom of Portugal|Portugal]], and left for [[East Asia]] in January 1684. His journey was funded by [[Maria de Guadalupe of Lencastre, 6th Duchess of Aveiro|Maria]], the [[duke of Aveiro|duchess]] of [[Aveiro, Portugal|Aveiro]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} He hoped to get passage to Japan on a [[Dutch East India Company]] [[Dutch missions to Edo|mission]], but in [[Dutch Malacca|Malacca]] he was assured by "Belgian Catholics from our cities" that this was impossible.<ref name=ruleno2/> 

He debarked at [[Portuguese Macau|Macau]] on 9 August 1685, where the return of some shipwrecked Japanese sailors caused him to hope that trade would be resumed; this was fruitless.<ref>{{harvp|Rule|2003|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA138 138–9]}}.</ref> He made his [[Four Solemn Vows|vows]] of [[poverty, chastity, obedience]], and the [[fourth vow]] of "special obedience" to the [[pope]] on 2 February the next year{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} and, after a final failed attempt to reach Japan,<ref name=ruleno3/> finally formally joined the [[Jesuit China missions|China mission]]{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} by September 1687.<ref name=ruleno3/> He is sometimes numbered among the [[Figurists]],{{sfnp|Lackner|1991|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=1OLN2M_BdkIC&pg=PA145 145]}} the Jesuit missionaries who came to think that Christianity had been the ancient religion of China, brought there by [[Noah]]'s son [[Shem]].

Noël learned rudimentary [[Chinese language|Chinese]] on Macau and traveled to the mainland in 1687. He traveled to [[Shanghai]],{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} then part of [[Jiangsu]] and—at nearby [[Xujiahui]]—the home of the family of the influential convert [[Xu Guangqi]]. After further training, he began his mission on nearby [[Chongming Island]] in early October 1688 and reported great success by August 1689:{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} 120 [[baptism|baptized]] converts in Shanghai, 300 on Chongming, and 800 in regions dependent on Chongming.<ref name=ruleno3>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA139 139]}}.</ref> 

From there, he travelled to [[Huai'an]] and [[Nanjing]] in [[Jiangsu]]; [[Wuhe County|Wuhe]] in [[Anhui]]; [[Nanchang]],{{efn|Shortly after leaving China, Noël reported to his patron the [[Maria de Guadalupe of Lencastre, 6th Duchess of Aveiro|Duchess of Aveiro]] that Nanchang averaged 400 converts a year during this period.<ref name=ruleno3/>}} [[Ganzhou]], [[Fuzhou, Jiangxi|Jianchang]] (now Fuzhou), and [[Nanfeng]] in [[Jiangxi]]; and [[Nan'an, Fujian|Nan'an]] in [[Fujian]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} 

A 1703 report to the Jesuit Provincial shows that Noël's work was primarily among the lower and working classes, especially to women and [[orphan|abandoned children]], which left open the problem of how to pay for church construction and mission work without resorting to begging for alms in the manner of the [[Buddhism in China|Buddhist]] [[bonzes|monks]].<ref name=ruleno4>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA140 140]}}.</ref>

===First Roman embassy===
[[File:Mandatum seu Edictum, Charles Maigrot.jpg|thumb|right|200px|[[Charles Maigrot]]'s 1693 ''Mandate'', which reopened the [[Chinese Rites controversy]]]]
[[File:P. Caspar Castner S.J.jpg|thumb|right|200px|[[Caspar Castner]], Noël's companion on his 1st embassy to Rome]]
{{further|Chinese Rites controversy}}
On 9 November 1701,<ref name=ruleno8>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA144 144]}}.</ref> he was selected—probably through the influence of his compatriot, the Vice Provincial Superior [[Antoine Thomas]]{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}}{{efn|Thomas and Noël apparently spent little time together but, apart from both being from the same area, they were both enthusiastic about reopening the Japan mission and worked together on improving the Jesuit maps of Japan, [[Zhongshan Island|Macau]], and [[Ayutthaya Kingdom|Thailand]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}}}}—to act as the [[Procurator (Catholic Church)|procurator]] for the China mission in an embassy concerning the [[Chinese Rites Controversy]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}} He was to argue on behalf of the Jesuits and four Chinese bishops that the [[Catholic Church]] should continue to permit the Chinese practice with [[Confucius|Confucian]] and [[ancestral veneration]] after their [[Christian conversion|conversion to Christianity]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=48}}

Thomas's letter reached him in Nanchang on the 25th; he left on 6 December and reached [[Guangzhou]] on 1 January.<ref name=ruleno8/> He was originally to travel with José Ramón Arxó and [[Claude de Visdelou]], but Arxó suffered accidental delays. Visdelou, meanwhile, was delayed first owing to reticence by the French mission to allow him to leave and then under various pretexts because the [[Canonical visitation|visitor]] Carlo Turcotti (correctly) suspected his position on the question of the rites.<ref name=ruleno8/> Since there was already an [[British East India Company|English]] ship ready to sail, Turcotti replaced the pair<ref>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA144 144–5]}}.</ref> with the [[Kingdom of Bavaria|Bavarian]] mathematician{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} [[Caspar Castner]], who was already working nearby.<ref name=ruleno9>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA145 145]}}.</ref> 

The English ship departed on 14 January 1702 for Macau, which it reached on the 21st and left on the 24th.<ref name=ruleno9/> It traveled to [[Batavia, Dutch East Indies|Batavia]] in the [[Dutch East Indies]] (now [[Jakarta]], [[Indonesia]]), where unbalanced cargo and heavy weather required a 17-day delay.<ref name=ruleno9/> On the journey around the [[Cape of Good Hope]], it was again held up for almost a month because of unfavorable winds.<ref name=ruleno9/> After a 43 day wait on [[Saint Helena]] owing to fear of a new European war, the ship passed through two storms to the [[Azores]] and through a collision off [[Calais]] to [[London]], which it reached on 4 October.<ref name=ruleno9/> The Jesuits met and presumably lobbied various ambassadors while in London, as well as the directors of the [[British East India Company|East India Company]].<ref name=ruleno9/> They crossed into France on the 31st, had an audience with [[Philip V of Spain|Philip V]] of [[Kingdom of Spain|Spain]] at [[Aix-en-Provence|Aix]], and passed from [[Marseille]] to [[Genoa]] on 15 December; they finally reached Rome on the 29th or 30th.<ref name=ruleno9/>

In Rome, the pair scheduled audiences, lobbied [[Catholic cardinal|cardinal]]s, prepared their documents, and attended sessions at the [[Holy Office]].<ref name=ruleno11>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA147 147]}}.</ref> They met [[Carlo Agostino Fabroni|Cardinal Fabroni]], the secretary of the [[Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith]] on 10 January 1703 and {{nowrap|[[Pope Clement XI]]}} two days later.<ref name=ruleno11/> On the 14th, they gave Fabroni the first round of documents: an overview, a dossier of verified testimony, books by [[João de Rocha|De Rocha]] and [[Giulio Alenio|Alenio]], and a 1664 anti-Christian pamphlet by [[Yang Guangxian]] whose complaints proved that the Jesuits were mentioning Jesus's [[crucifixion of Jesus|crucifixion]] to the Chinese.<ref name=ruleno11/> Some of these were rejected on various grounds, and they were forced to hire a lawyer surnamed Ursaia to present them in the proper format around March.<ref name=ruleno11/> The [[Order of Friars Minor|Franciscan]] [[Giovanni Francesco Nicolai da Leonessa]] had been opposing them before their arrival; on 10 March he was joined by the [[Paris Foreign Missions Society|MEP]] missionary [[Artus de Lionne]].<ref name=ruleno11/>

Despite the Noël and Castner's efforts negotiating the Roman bureaucracy over the next two years, the voluminous Chinese testimony—including an official pronouncement by the [[Kangxi Emperor]]—on the respectful but not worshipful nature of [[ancestral veneration|Chinese veneration]], and the pains the Jesuits undertook transmitting it around the French mission in [[Nanjing]] (which supposedly intercepted it under orders from [[Charles Maigrot|Bishop Maigrot]]),<ref name=ruleno10>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA146 146]}}.</ref> there is no evidence that the Roman court ever weighed any of the Jesuit evidence.<ref name=ruleno10/> Instead, despite the pope's kind words,<ref name=ruleno15/> the decision had already been reached well ahead of its formal proclamation: [[Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon]] had been named [[papal legate|legate]] for China and the East Indies on 5 December 1701 with the specific instructions to disallow further practice of Chinese rituals by Christians there;{{sfnp|Ott|1913}}<ref name=ruleno13>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA149 149]}}.</ref> he was given [[Papal legate#Legatus a latere|papal-like supremacy]] over the clerics there and, on the 27th, consecrated as the [[titular see|titular]] [[patriarch of Antioch]],{{sfnp|Ott|1913}} making him the notional head of the churches across most of Asia. He left for the Qing Empire aboard the French ship ''Maurepas'' on 9 February 1703, only weeks after Noël's arrival, and disallowed the Jesuit leniency towards to the [[Malabar rites]] while he waited out the [[monsoon season]] in [[French India|Pondicherry]].{{sfnp|Ott|1913}} By 1704, Noël and Castner were forbidden from publishing their arguments, although their opponents were printing their treatises in great volume, and correspondence and treatises shipped from China were confiscated at [[Livorno]].<ref name=ruleno15/> Noël seems to have accepted that there was little to be done or been otherwise occupied for the rest of the year.<ref name=ruleno15>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA151 151]}}.</ref> Castner continued his lobbying, assisted after 26 February 1704 by [[Jean-François de Pélisson]], who arrived with further documentation from the Jesuits in China.<ref name=ruleno15/>

[[File:Portrait of the Kangxi Emperor in Court Dress.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Aixinjueluo Xuanye, the [[Kangxi Emperor]] of the [[Qing dynasty|Qing]] <small>(18th{{nbsp}}c.)</small>]]
On 20 November [[Pope Clement XI|Pope Clement{{nbsp}}XI]]'s [[papal decree|decree]] {{lang|la|[[Cum Deus Optimus]]...}} ruled almost completely against the Jesuits,<ref name=ruleno16>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA152 152]}}.</ref> formalizing a ban on both the rites and further discussion of the topic. Christians could not refer to [[Christian God|God]] as {{lang|zh|{{linktext|天}}}} (''tiān'', "[[Tian|Heaven]]" or "the sky") and their churches could not display the imperial plaque ordering parishioners to "Revere Heaven" ({{lang|zh|{{linktext|敬|天}}}}, ''Jìng Tiān'').<ref name=ruleno16/> [[Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon|Tournon]] was to prepare more detailed regulations to avoid "every hint of pagan superstition",<ref name=ruleno16/> and the decree was worded legalistically and carefully—"hall or temple", "sacrifice or offering"—to limit any chance the Jesuits might evade or limit its application.<ref name=sirrah>{{harvp|Seah|2017|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=sOEzDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA115 115]}}.</ref>

Noël returned east in 1706, traveling—at Castner's insistence—not via [[Portuguese Goa|Goa]] and through the [[Straits of Malacca]] but around [[Timor]]; this route proved faster and subsequently became standard for journeys between Europe and [[Portuguese Macau|Macau]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} They arrived on 22 July 1707,{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} finding the [[papal legate|legate]] [[Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon|Tournon]] under arrest in Macau{{sfnp|Ott|1913}} and the entire mission in chaos. The sickly Tournon had arrived at Macau in April 1705{{sfnp|Zhang|2006|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=o_u2P83LgGUC&pg=PA146 146]}} and Beijing on 4 December,<ref name=wakeup>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA257 257]}}.</ref> insisting on the incompatibility of [[Confucianism]] and [[Roman Catholicism]].{{sfnp|Von Collani|2009|p=2}} His first imperial audience the same month had been diplomatic and held out hope for [[China–Holy See relations|permanent relations]] between China and the [[Papal States]];<ref name=wakeup/> his second, on 29 June 1706, had found the emperor displeased that any controversy had arisen over the Jesuits' accommodation of rites he had personally verified as secular<ref name=comewithuscharby/> and, in any case, necessary for Chinese society.<ref name=isthemeadowonfire>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA258 258–9]}}.</ref> Tournon—still generally uninformed on the details of the situation<ref name=wakeup/> — had deferred to the "great expert" Maigrot, whose analysis had prompted Rome's reversal, and the emperor agreed to receive him at the new [[Chengde Mountain Resort|summer palace]] at Rehe (now [[Chengde]]).<ref name=maptocandymountain>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA259 259]}}.</ref> Maigrot had already been summoned from Fujian<ref name=sirrah/> and was interviewed on 2 August 1706.{{sfnp|Von Collani|2009|p=3}} Despite having lived in China since 1684,{{sfnp|Von Collani|2009|p=2}} he proved so grossly ignorant — he knew only [[Fuzhounese]]<ref name=archer>{{harvp|Zhang|2006|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=o_u2P83LgGUC&pg=PA147 147]}}</ref> and required [[Dominique Parrenin]] to translate the emperor's questions.<ref name=maptocandymountain/> He claimed to have read the [[Four Books]] but was unable to remember two characters from them by heart;<ref name=maptocandymountain/> he had not even read [[Matteo Ricci]]'s [[Tianzhu Shiyi|Chinese catechism]];{{sfnp|Ricci|1603}}<ref name=sirrah/> and he could read only one of the four [[Chinese character]]s on the plaque behind the emperor's head<ref name=archer/> but presumed to lecture the patron of the [[Kangxi Dictionary]] on the permissible meanings of the character {{lang|zh|{{linktext|天}}}};<ref name=comewithuscharby>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA260 260]}}.</ref>—and stubborn<ref name=adventure>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA261 261]}}.</ref> that he had finally been expelled from the country on 17 December {{sfnp|Von Collani|2009|p=3}} and Christian missionaries required to receive an imperial permit ({{lang|zh|{{linktext|票}}}}, ''piào'') attesting to their support of "the method of [[Matteo Ricci]]" and their willingness to remain in China for the rest of their lives.<ref name=liopleurodon>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA262 262]}}.</ref>{{sfnp|Von Collani|2009|p=3}} Finally receiving notice of {{lang|la|Cum Deus Optimus...}},<ref name=liopleurodon/> 

Tournon had ordered a [[latae sententiae|summary and automatic]] [[excommunication]] of any Christian permitting Confucian rituals from [[Nanjing]] on 25 January 1707;{{sfnp|Ott|1913}} on 7 February, he had further issued instructions concerning the ''piao'' examination—again on pain of excommunication<ref name=liopleurodon/> — that precluded its ever being approved.<ref name=sirrah/> Enraged, the emperor finally had him arrested and deported on 13 June,<ref name=shunthenonbeliever>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA262 262–3]}}.</ref> with the [[Portuguese Empire|Portuguese]] then holding him under [[house arrest]] for their own reasons.<ref name=bridgeofhopeandwonder>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA263 263]}}.</ref>

===Second Roman Embassy===
[[File:Open letter from Kangxi to Pope Clement XI.png|thumb|200px|right|The [[Kangxi Emperor]]'s 1716 [[open letter]] to [[Pope Clement XI|Clement{{nbsp}}XI]], inquiring about the fate of his 1706 and 1708 embassies]]
About half of the missionaries then in China joined [[Charles Maigrot|Maigrot]] and [[Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon|Tournon]] in exile.<ref name=heycharby>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA256 256] & [https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA262 262]}}.</ref> At the emperor's insistence, a second embassy was dispatched to Rome to overturn {{lang|la|Cum Deus Optimus...}} and Maigrot and Tournon's various rulings in 1706; this was apparently lost at sea.<ref name=bridgeofhopeandwonder/> Unable to secure a residence permit without fear of [[excommunication]], Noël joined a third embassy. (He has sometimes been said to have been specifically requested by the [[Kangxi Emperor]], although this seems unlikely.)<ref name=ruleno16/>

Noël departed for Europe from Macau on 14 January 1708 on the [[Kingdom of Portugal|Portuguese]] ship ''Bom Jesus de Mazagão das Brotas'' with the Jesuits José Ramón Arxó and António Francesco Giuseppe Provana and the Chinese convert [[Louis Fan (convert)|Louis Fan]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} Traveling via [[Batavia, Dutch East Indies|Batavia]] and [[Bahia]], [[Portuguese Brazil|Brazil]], they arrived in [[Lisbon]] in September and in Rome by February the next year.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} En route, he sent a letter ahead to the pope imploring:<ref name=ruleno17>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA153 153]}}.</ref>

{{blockquote|It is all up with this once flourishing mission now collapsing, and rushing to certain ruin, unless [[Pope Clement XI|Your Holiness]] should please the [[Kangxi Emperor|emperor of the Chinese]] by a swift response, and graciously agree to his requests regarding the Chinese rites so long in dispute.}}

[[Pope Clement XI|Clement]] supported Tournon completely.<ref name=candymtn>{{harvp|Charbonnier|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=5yUzntxTZioC&pg=PA264 264]}}.</ref> A [[papal decree|decree]] from the [[Holy Office]] was issued on 25 September 1710 upholding all of his rules and condemnations.<ref name=candymtn/> The embassy may have been enjoined from sending the Kangxi Emperor any notice of that fact, since he never learned the fate of either of his embassies; in 1716, he resorted to providing open letters (the "Red Manifesto")<ref name=ruleno16/> to passing European merchants to try to ascertain their fate.{{sfnp|Rosso|1948|pp=307–9}} (Noël, however, was not one of those individually listed for the merchants to search for.)<ref name=ruleno16/>

===In Europe===
[[File:Clementinum_baroque_library_2.jpg|thumb|200px|The [[Czech National Library]], formerly the [[Clementinum]] Library of [[Charles-Ferdinand University]], completed in the 1720s]]
Noël then appears to have moved to [[Prague]], in the [[Austrian Empire]]'s [[Kingdom of Bohemia]] (now the [[Czech Republic]]). There, he published mathematical and astronomical observations from [[Portuguese India|India]] and [[Qing Empire|China]]{{sfnp|Noël|1710}} and [[lecturer|lectured]] on mathematics at the Jesuit-staffed [[Charles-Ferdinand University]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} He also published [[Neo-Latin|Latin]] translations of [[Confucian classics|classic Chinese texts]]{{sfnp|Noël|1711}} and works on [[Sinology]] which he had worked over for decades.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} Noël's translations were banned in the [[Papal States]] and [[Holy Roman Empire]], but were praised by [[Jean-Baptiste Du Halde|Du Halde]] in his ''[[Description of China]]''.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}}<ref name=mungo>{{harvp|Mungello|1991|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=1OLN2M_BdkIC&pg=PA107 107]}}.</ref> They were difficult to acquire in France and western Europe but were among the most influential Jesuit works in Germany and eastern Europe,<ref name=mungojerry>{{harvp|Mungello|1991|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=1OLN2M_BdkIC&pg=PA107 107–8]}}.</ref> where they inspired works by [[Johann Benedikt Carpzov]],<ref name=knud/> [[Wilhelm von Leibnitz]], and [[Christian Wolff (philosopher)|Christian Wolff]],{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} the latter of whom lost his position at the [[University of Halle]] because of his immoderate praise of [[Confucius]] and admission that the Chinese had been able to [[ethics|distinguish between right and wrong]] without exposure to Christianity. Noël's ''Historical Notices''—which aimed to reopen the Chinese rites issue—does not seem to have been formally banned but was almost immediately suppressed.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=51}} It seems likely that its claimed papal [[imprimatur]] was that which [[Pope Clement XI|Clement]] had granted to publish findings ''before'' his 1704 decision;{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=51}} on 19 March 1715, he issued the [[papal bull|bull]] {{lang|la|[[Ex Illa Die]]...}} repeating in stronger terms his condemnations and the incompatibility of Chinese ritual with Catholicism.

On 10 June that year, Noël sought approval to return to China{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=51}} although he was 64 at the time. He was denied permission.<ref name=ruleno1>{{harvp|Rule|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Dw9gYo4Pk0MC&pg=PA137 137]}}.</ref> He died on 17 September 1729 in [[Lille]], [[Kingdom of France|France]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=51}}

==Works==
[[File:LifeAndWorksOfConfucius1687.jpg|thumb|right|200px|The engraving of [[Confucius]] in the 1687 ''[[Confucius Sinarum Philosophus|Confucius, Philosopher of the Chinese]]''. Noël's own translations had no illustrations, apart from their floral tailpieces.]]
Noël published his ''Mathematical and Physical Observations Made in India and China'' ({{langx|la|Observationes Mathematicae et Physicae in India et China Factae}}) at the [[Charles-Ferdinand University]]'s press in [[Prague]], [[Kingdom of Bohemia|Bohemia]] (now the [[Czech Republic]]), in 1710.{{sfnp|Noël|1710}}

Noël's effort to translate the Chinese classics was a generally scholarly one, aiming to present it more correctly on its own terms than previous Jesuit editions like the ''[[Confucius Sinarum Philosophus]]'' had,{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=50}}<ref name=knud/>{{sfnp|Schonfeld|2003|p=27}} but it was still an exercise undertaken in order to further [[Christian mission|missionizing]] among the Chinese.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=46}} The preface to his ''Six Chinese Classics'' ends with the admonition that the reader should bear the [[Christian culture|Christian life]] in mind while reading the volume's [[Confucianism|Chinese teachings]] and the hope that the work would assist in making [[Jesus Christ|Christ]] the cornerstone to every life.{{sfnp|Noël|1711|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=A0K0bjBLmMYC&pg=PP11 xi]}} The Jesuits initially focused on translating [[Confucian classics]], rather than [[Buddhist scripture]]s or the [[Taoist canon]], because of its greater importance in [[scholar-bureaucrat|Chinese officialdom]] under the [[Ming dynasty|Ming]] and [[Qing dynasty|Qing]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=46}} The [[Mengzi (book)|works]] of [[Mencius]] were not originally translated because [[Matteo Ricci]] disliked Mencian interpretations of the other classic texts, particularly his strong condemnation of [[clerical celibacy|celibacy]] as [[filial piety|unfilial]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=47}}

Noël published his ''Six Classic Books of the Chinese Empire'' ({{lang|la|Sinensis Imperii Libri Classici Sex}}) at the same press the next year,{{sfnp|Noël|1711}} although his manuscripts show he had been working on them since at least 1700.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}} The six classics were the ''[[Great Learning]]'' ({{langx|la|Adultorum Schola}} or {{lang|la|Doctrina}}),{{sfnp|Noël|1711|pp=1–29}} the ''[[Doctrine of the Mean]]'' ({{lang|la|Immutabile Medium}}),{{sfnp|Noël|1711|pp=31–73}} the ''[[Analects]]'' ({{lang|la|Liber Sententiarum}}),{{sfnp|Noël|1711|pp=75–198}} the [[Mengzi (book)|collected works]] of [[Mencius]] ({{lang|la|Memcius}}<!--sic-->),{{sfnp|Noël|1711|pp=199–472}} the ''[[Classic of Filial Piety]]'' ({{lang|la|Filialis Observantia}}),{{sfnp|Noël|1711|pp=473–484}} and the ''[[Lesser Learning]]'' ({{lang|la|Parvulorum Schola}}).{{sfnp|Noël|1711|pp=485–608}}{{sfnp|Schonfeld|2003|p=27}} Each of the first four are completely new translations prefaced by [[Zhu Xi]]'s [[Sishu Jizhu|commentaries]] (<small>[[traditional characters|t]]</small>{{nbsp}}{{lang|zh|{{linktext|四書|集注}}}}, <small>[[simplified characters|s]]</small>{{nbsp}}{{lang|zh|{{linktext|四书|集注}}}}, ''Sìshū Jízhù'').{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=50}}<ref name=knud>{{harvp|Lundbæk|1991|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=1OLN2M_BdkIC&pg=PA39 39]}}.</ref> Each of the last three were the first European translations of the works.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=50}} All were rather fairly freely translated from the editions established by Zhu Xi; his preface states the works are "not, so to speak, what the Chinese wrote but, I hope, what they really meant".{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=50}}{{efn|{{langx|la|"...non tantum ut discas, quae Sinae scripserunt, set et ut agas, quae recte senserunt..."}}{{sfnp|Noël|1711|p=i}}}} For example, the first lines of the ''Doctrine of the Mean'' were rendered "The [[Mandate of Heaven|Law]] of [[Tian|Heaven]] is nature itself; the tendency of this nature is the [[Tao|way of acting correctly]]; the direction of this life is a right discipline of life, or the right precepts for living."{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=50}}{{efn|{{langx|la|"Caeli lex est ipsa natura; hujus naturae ductus est recta agendi via; hujus viae directio est recta vitae disciplina, seu recta vivendi praecepta..."}}{{sfnp|Noël|1711|p=41}}}}

At the same time, he published his ''Three Treatises on Chinese Philosophy'' ({{lang|la|Philosophia Sinica Tribus Tractatibus}}).{{sfnp|Noël|1711b}} Its three sections deal with "On Knowledge of the First Being or God among the Chinese" ({{lang|la|De Cognitione Primi Entis seu Dei apud Sinas}}), "On the Ceremonies of the Chinese for the Dead" ({{lang|la|De Ceremoniis Sinarum erga Denunctos}}), and "On Chinese Ethics" ({{lang|la|De Ethica Sinensi}}).{{sfnp|Noël|1711b}} Unlike earlier Jesuit works, it does not claim that the [[Neo-Confucianism]] of [[Zhu Xi]] and others was a [[Buddhism in China|Buddhist]] corruption of [[Confucianism]]; it treats it as an organic development although still cautioning that its vague terms should not be used in reference to the [[Christian God]].{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=49}}

Finally, in the same year, he also published ''Historical Notices of Chinese Rituals and Ceremonies in the Veneration of Deceased Parents and Benefactors''.{{sfnp|Noël|1711c}} It expands on the topic of the second his ''Three Treatises'', with many more citations from Chinese works.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=51}} Combatively [[polemic]]al in describing an understanding of [[Chinese ancestral veneration]] that is compatible with [[Roman Catholicism|Catholicism]], it claimed a papal [[imprimatur]] for its publishing but was almost immediately suppressed.{{sfnp|Liščák|2015|p=51}}

He published his ''Little Poetic Works'' ({{lang|la|Opuscula Poetica}}) at [[Frankfurt-on-Main|Frankfurt]] in 1717.{{sfnp|Noël|1717}} Its four parts comprise a ''Life of Jesus Christ under the Name of Divine Love'' ({{lang|la|Vita Jesu Christi sub Nomine Divini Amoris}});{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA1 1–86]}} ''Marian Letters'' ({{lang|la|Epistolae Marianae}});{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA87 87–136]}} a ''Life of St Ignatius of Loyola, Founder of the Jesuits'' ({{lang|la|Vita Sancti Ignatii de Loyola Societatis Jesu Fundatoris}});{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA137 137–213]}} and several tragedies ({{lang|la|Tragoediae}}), including ''Philotas'',{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA214 214–255]}} ''Herod'' ({{lang|la|Herodes}}),{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA256 256–295]}} ''Love'' ({{lang|la|Amor}}),{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA296 296–338]}} ''Lucifer'',{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA339 339–391]}} ''Accianus'',{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA392 392–428]}} and ''Henry'' ({{lang|la|Henricus}}).{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA429 429–461]}} An appendix includes the comedy ''Blind Sight'' ({{lang|la|Caecus Videns}}).{{sfnp|Noël|1717|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BmATAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA462 462 ff]}}

He also published a popular theology textbook.<ref name=ruleno1/>
